families.name: Bantu
families.description: Largest language family in Kenya (~65% of population). Spread across central, western, and coastal regions.

families.name: Nilotic
families.description: Second largest family (~30%). Includes Plains Nilotes (Maasai, Turkana, Samburu, Teso), Highland Nilotes (Kalenjin, Pokot), and River-Lake Nilotes (Luo).

families.name: Cushitic
families.description: Found in northern and eastern Kenya (~3%). Includes Somali, Borana/Oromo, Rendille, and Daasanach (Dhaasanac).

families.name: Other
families.description: Includes Swahili (Bantu-based national & official lingua franca), English (official), and minor language isolates.

languages.name: Kikuyu (Gĩkũyũ)
languages.notes: Largest mother-tongue community in the central highlands (Kiambu/Kabeti, Murang'a/Metumi/Fort Hall, and Nyeri/Gaki around Mount Kenya [Kĩrĩnyaga / Kĩreĩra]); documented in Höhnel (1894), Hémery (1903), Hinde (1904), McGregor (1904), W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa'), Hobley (1910, 1922), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Dholuo (Luo)
languages.notes: River-Lake Nilotes of the Lake Victoria basin; documented in Rev. Charles New (1873), Rev. Thomas Wakefield & Robert Needham Cust (1883 'A Sketch of the Modern Languages of Africa', Vol. I, Ch. XI.D 'Nile Sub-Group', pp. 273–287: XXI. Kavirondo on Victoria Nyanza pp. 284–285, Wakefield's MS Kavirondo Vocabulary from a Swahíli caravan traveller, and first comparative proof of marked affinity with I. Shilluk/Dyur [Luoh/Lwo, Bellanda & Dembo] pp. 275–276, XVIII. Lúr [Luoh] pp. 282–283 & XX. Shúli [Gani/Shefalu] pp. 283–284), Hobley (1902, 1903), Johnston (1902), Northcote (1907), Roscoe/Willis (1915), Mill-Hill Fathers (1920), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Kalenjin
languages.notes: Highland Nilotes (Nandi, Kipsigis/Lumbwa [Il Kakesan], Tugen/Kamasia [Kapteberewa & Nderois], Marakwet & Endo/Ndo [Chebleng], Keiyo/Elgeyo, Cherang'any, Kabkamat/Olmo, Sangwirr, Uasin Gishu Moiven/Muttia/Il-Mokwan/I-Sirikwa, Sabaot, Pökoot); documented in Hobley (1902, 1903, 1910), Johnston (1902), A. C. Hollis (1909 'The Nandi: Their Language and Folk-Lore'), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Beech (1911), BFBS (1921), Rottland (1982), Creider & Creider (1983, 1989), Toweett (1979), Mietzner (2016), Jerono (2018), Sitienei Jepkoech (2018), Diercks & Rao (2019), Landman (2019), Kouneli (2021), and Joost Zwarts, Andrew Chelimo & Prisca Jerono (2023; 2024 'The reflexive in Kalenjin: Its syntactic status and semantic functions', in Yaqian Huang, Nina Hagen Kaldhol, Jun Jie Lim, Sharon Rose & Anthony Struthers-Young, eds., ACAL in SoCAL: Selected papers from the 53rd Annual Conference on African Linguistics, Berlin: Language Science Press, Ch. 21, pp. 539–556, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.11210482 — audited 100% line-by-line across §§1–7, 1,815 Endo-Marakwet NT occurrences of keey [1,653 separate-word tokens + 162 in karkeey, cheepaykeey & peerkeey], Examples 1–24, Footnotes 1–12, 5 Abbreviations & 17 References).

languages.name: Luhya (Luyia)
languages.notes: 17+ Western Bantu dialects including Wanga (Luhanga of Buhanga), Bukusu/Masaba, Kabras, Nyala, Marama, Tsotso, Tiriki, Idakho, Isukha, and Maragoli (Logoori); documented in Hobley (1902, 1903), Johnston (1902, 1919), Purvis (1907, 1909), Roscoe (1915), Rev. N. Stam (1929 'The Bahanga', Catholic Anthropological Conference Vol. I, No. 4, pp. 143–179 — audited 100% line-by-line across the p. 145 Map, 11-generation Bakhitsetse royal genealogy from Kwandedi & Wanga to Mumia, Osundwa II & Rapando, royal sitting burial & Matungo bone procession, Fig. 1 commoner burial diagram, Fig. 2 kraal sacrificial stones & khatsu khe misango diagram, reversive -ula, 5 special sacrifices, khyembekho rainmaking, Nasayi/Were prayers & Chameleon myth, 6 practitioners, 2 ordeals, 10 omens, Makokha adoption, amakhwana twin rites, okhutekherana marriage, musiro totems & okhukhyebwa circumcision), and Payne, Pacchiarotti & Bosire eds. (2016).

languages.name: Kamba (Kĩkamba)
languages.notes: Central Bantu language of Eastern Kenya across 4 regional divisions (Ulu/Yulu [kīkamba kīluŋgalu & Kīluŋgu], East Ukamba/Kitui [aþaisu / kīþaisu], Kīkumbuliu & Mumonī, plus Anoka on Mt. Noka and the 1836 Rabai diaspora); documented in Krapf (1850), Last (1885), Hinde (1904), Hobley (1910, 1922), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), Gerhard Lindblom (1920 'The Akamba in British East Africa: An Ethnological Monograph', 2nd Ed., Enlarged, Archives d'Études Orientales Vol. 17, Uppsala, pp. I–XII, 1–607, Figs. 1–167 — audited 100% line-by-line across all 35 chapters, Addenda, 7 informants, 25+ mbaī clans & brands [Figs. 17–51], 3 nžaīko initiations, musaī sticks [Figs. 1–8] & sand drawings [Figs. 9–16], nðonī & 11 kwiūa pairs, 7 women's words, kinship table, 5 atumīa meat-sharing grades, nsīlī law, kīþītū [Fig. 52] & ndundu oaths, 6 ordeals, kīŋgolə, 3 war divisions & mutīætumo honours, aīmu, īþæmbo & Muluŋgu/Mumbī/Mwatwaŋgagī prayers, kuausīa divination, unīka/mwītano arch, 17 ŋgondu substances, 45+ medicinal plants, 9 famines, 3 11-month calendars, kuseuβīa maīo teeth-chipping & bone false teeth, 11 musical instruments, kīūīśī board game, 13-part hut plan [Fig. 125], 7 traps, 28 livestock terms, mwatu beekeeping, munīo S-link chains & 3 color roots), BFBS (1921), and Jones & Freyer (2019).

languages.name: Somali
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic language of North Eastern Kenya; documented in Rigby (1850, 1866), Burton (1856), Hunter (1880), Robert Needham Cust (1883 'A Sketch of the Modern Languages of Africa', Vol. I, Ch. IX.C.I 'Somáli', pp. 119, 121: Reinisch's First Ethiopic-Hamitic Cluster [Bishári, Saho, Dankálí, Somáli, Galla], Regio Aromatifera from Bab el Mandal & Cape Guardafui to the Bantu frontier, and Krapf's testimony that the Somáli 'consist of a multitude of tribes speaking one Language'), de Larajasse (1897), Kirk (1903, 1905), BFBS (1921), Nilsson (2016), Kimper et al. (2019), and Nurse (2019).

languages.name: Kisii (Ekegusii)
languages.notes: Eastern Lake Victoria Bantu language of the Kisii Highlands; documented in Hobley (1902) and Johnston (1902, 1919).

languages.name: Meru (Kĩmĩĩrũ)
languages.notes: Mount Kenya & Tana valley Bantu cluster (Imenti, Tigania, Igembe, Mwimbi, Chuka, and Kĩtharaka); documented in Hobley (1910), Champion (1912), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), and Kithaka wa Mberia (2004).

languages.name: Maasai (Maa)
languages.notes: Plains Nilotes (Eastern Nilotic, across 4 Clans ['L-Aiser, Il-Meñgana, Il-Mokesen, Il-Molelyan], 2 Moieties ['L-oodo-kishu & 'L-oorook-kishu], 19 Sub-Families [Il-gilat], and 5 Districts [Il-Kaputiei, En-aiposha, 'L-Oitai, Il-Kisonko, 'L-Uasinkishu], plus Laikipiak, Segellai, and Tigirri); documented in Krapf (1854 'Vocabulary of the Engútuk Eloikób'), Erhardt & Krapf (1857 'Vocabulary of the Enguduk Iloigob'), Farler & Wakefield (1882), Robert Needham Cust (1883 'A Sketch of the Modern Languages of Africa', Vol. I, Ch. X.A.V–VI 'Kwáfi' & 'Masai', pp. 149–152: autonyms Loikób/Eloikób 'Men', J. T. Last's 6,000-word Humba vocabulary at Mamboia, Arúsha & Ndorobo 'Helot Races', Joseph Thomson's 1883 RGS expedition supplied by Cust, and Lepsius's 1880 6 structural features), Höhnel (1894), Hildegarde Hinde (1901 'The Masai Language: Grammatical Notes Together with a Vocabulary' — audited 100% line-by-line across pp. i–xii, 1–75 [PDF pp. 1–98]), Johnston (1902), A. C. Hollis & Sir Charles Eliot (1905 'The Masai: Their Language and Folklore' — audited 100% line-by-line across Parts I–VI, pp. i–xxviii, 1–359, Frontispiece & Plates I–XXVII), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Hobley (1910), W. S. & K. Routledge (1910, Appendix II pp. 344–349 & Plate CXXXVI), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Turkana (Ng'aturukana)
languages.notes: Plains Nilotes (Ateker branch: 16 principal tribes and 19 Ngoitunya & Ngolio attegir clans); documented in Höhnel (1894), Johnston (1902), Purvis (1909), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Beech (1911), and Barton (1921).

languages.name: Embu (Kĩembu)
languages.notes: Mount Kenya southeastern slopes (Embu & Mbeere); documented in Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), and Hobley (1922).

languages.name: Taita (Kidawida)
languages.notes: Taita Hills Bantu (Dawida, Sagala, Kasigau); documented in Shaw (1885), Taylor (1891), Wray (1894), Werner (1915), Johnston (1919), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Swahili (Kiswahili)
languages.notes: National & official language of Kenya (including Kiamu, Kimvita, Kitikuu/Bajuni, Kipate, Kingozi, and Kiunguja); documented in Krapf (1850, 1882), Bishop Edward Steere (1870 'Swahili Tales, as Told by Natives of Zanzibar', Bell & Daldy London, pp. i–xvi, 1–504 [PDF pp. 1–529] — audited 100% line-by-line across J. F. Campbell's Aug. 1, 1870 provenance & Kalila and Dimna marginalia, 6 named informants, 3 Mombasa Preface poems, 18 prose tales incl. Kimvita 'Kititi, na Fisi, na Simba' & 'Hadithi ya Liongo', all 20 verbatim Mifano, all 14 Vitendawili, 'Mashairi ya Liongo', 'Utumbuizo wa Gungu', 'Mwanzo wa Utenzi wa Ayubu', all 37 Italicized Words, all 103 Notes & all 12 Corrigenda), Robert Needham Cust (1883 'A Sketch of the Modern Languages of Africa', Vol. I, pp. 11–16, 42–43, 48, 54, 74, 76–77, 84–85, 119, 211: Zanzibár Omanite Arabic per Prætorius, Sawáhil/Káfir/Kabáil/Zinjian etymologies, Indian Bhattia/Borah/Khoja traders keeping accounts in Gujaráti & Kachchi from Zanzibár to Cape Guardafui, Steere's critique of Bagamóyo pidgin Swahili, East Coast Arabic script vs. Krapf/Steere/Lepsius Roman orthographies, and Frere Town freed-slave vocabulary appeal), Bishop Edward Steere & A. C. Madan (1894 'A Handbook of the Swahili Language, as Spoken at Zanzibar', 4th Ed., SPCK London, pp. i–xxii, 1–458 [PDF pp. 1–488] — audited 100% line-by-line; plus 1918), Taylor (1891), Bateman (1901), A. C. Madan (1903 'Swahili-English Dictionary', Clarendon Press Oxford, pp. i–xix, 1–442 [PDF pp. 1–478] — audited 100% line-by-line; plus 1902, 1905, 1917), Mrs. F. Burt & Rev. W. E. Taylor (1910 'Swahili Grammar and Vocabulary', SPCK London, pp. 1–252 [PDF pp. 1–260] — audited 100% line-by-line), Stigand (1915), Beech (1918), Werner (1918, 1919, 1933), Mohamed Mwamzandi (2022 'The pragmatics of Swahili relative clauses', Language Science Press, Ch. 13, pp. 227–246, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.6393758 — audited 100% line-by-line across all 440 HCS 2.0 relative clauses, Examples 1–32, Figure 1 & Tables 1–2), and Goldsmith & Mpiranya (2022).

languages.name: Mijikenda
languages.notes: Nine coastal Sabaki sub-groups (Giriama, Digo, Duruma, Chonyi, Jibana, Kambe, Ribe, Rabai, Kauma); documented in Krapf (1850), Krapf & Rebmann (1887), Taylor (1891), Werner (1915), Johnston (1919), BFBS (1921), and Nicolle (2016).

languages.name: Borana (Oromo)
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic language (Borana [including the Royal Clan Karayu of Chief Gedu in Ethiopia], Gabbra, Sakuye, Wata, and Tana River Orma — Barareta Oromo [descended from Ana Bake], Kofira Oromo [from Ana Dima/Ana Bake], and Migo Oromo [from Ana Kare]); documented in Krapf (1840, 1842, 1850), Tutschek (1844–1845), Robert Needham Cust (1883 'A Sketch of the Modern Languages of Africa, Accompanied by a Language-Map', Vol. I, London: Trübner & Co., pp. [i]–xvi, 1–287 [PDF pp. 1–340] — audited 100% line-by-line across Portrait Plates I–VI [31 portraits], Chs. I–XI, and Ch. IX.C.II 'Galla or Orómo' pp. 122–125: 5–6 million speakers from 10° N to the Dana/Tana River mouth near Mombása, Huma royal dynasty of Uganda/Unyoro/Karagwe, autonym Orma/Oromo 'men' vs. war-title 'Sons of Galla', 5 Chief Dialects incl. the Equatorial/Tana River dialect studied by Wakefield at Ribé & Krapf 1850, Charles New's Wata 'Helot Races', Cust's hand-copied MS of Krapf's 1840 Elements sent to Wakefield at Ribé, Newman, Bleek, Massaia, Tutschek, Enaréa & Lango/Kidi), Foot (1913), Werner (1915), BFBS (1921), Mikael Samson & R. G. Darroch (1944, pp. 370–394), and Griefenow-Mewis (1996).

languages.name: Rendille
languages.notes: Omo-Tana East Cushitic camel-herding pastoralists of the Kaisut and Chalbi plains (including the historical Naroshon section on the Sogota–Lomello plains); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Höhnel (1894), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Hobley (1910), Fleming (1964), and Heine (1976).

languages.name: Teso (Ateso)
languages.notes: Eastern Nilotic (Ateker) language spoken in Busia County and eastern Uganda; documented in Hobley (1902), Johnston (1902), Purvis (1909), Kitching (1915), Roscoe (1915), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Pokomo
languages.notes: Tana River (Galana Maro) Sabaki Bantu language across Malachini (Kalindi [Namboo & Mangwe/Gomeni], Buu, Yunda/Dzunza, Ngatana, Kulesa, Mwina) and Upper Pokomo (Ndera, Gwano, Kinakomba, Ndura, Zubaki, Malalulu — bordered on the north by the non-Pokomo Elwana and Munyo); documented in Krapf (1850), Würtz (1895, 1896), Werner (1913, 1915, 1933), Johnston (1919–1922 #13 Pωkωmω), BFBS (1921), and Mikael Samson & R. G. Darroch (1944 'A History of the Pokomo by Mikael Samson — Continued, with an Introduction and Notes by R. G. Darroch', Journal of the East Africa Natural History Society, Vol. XVII, Nos. 5 & 6 [79–80], Sept. 1944, pp. 370–394 & Full-Page Sketch Map — audited 100% line-by-line across all 14 map sections from Elwana to Ras Shaka, Hidabo Hill [Mrio / Kina Inti], Shaka [Waungwana wa Mashaa, A.H. 121], Liongo Fumo & Ozi, family mlango land tenure, the 3 dried Buu rivers [Milaoni/Magogoni with Sanye hippo covenant, Ngambwa with Chikovu & 1941 Kopole/Mihaja forest award, and Mbewee], the verbatim 8-line Kipokomo lament song for Chikovu on p. 385, all 6 Upper Pokomo tribes and their Bantu/Oromo clan tables, Sango Vere & Ana Dima's 'Abamogo' wayfarer greeting at Lake Lemu/Mitole, the Treacherous War of Jilo Bune & Chief Dadho Moroa, the Battles of Kirungu [Buya Gafo & Mwenye Era] & Kadada [Karayu Wayu, Goyoi & Malim Jilo], Chief Mukaraji Maro's 6-generation genealogy, Ngaji/Kijo forest guardians, 7th-month pregnancy farming exemption, Waganga, Muunguni heaven & 'God's portion', Missions 1884–1887, Islam, 1895 arrival of first D.C. Mr. Anderssen 'Bwana Muchinjeni' at Ngao, and Notes 1–13).

languages.name: Samburu
languages.notes: Northern Maa (Plains Nilotic) pastoralists (including historical Il Doigio, Lorogishu / Kwakituk on Angata e-'m-barta, and Lobbeyok sections); documented in Krapf (1854), Farler & Wakefield (1882), Cust (1883, Vol. I, pp. 149–152), Höhnel (1894), Johnston (1902), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), and Hobley (1910).

languages.name: Ilchamus (Njemps)
languages.notes: Lake Baringo Maa-speaking irrigation farmers and fishermen (Njamus / Nyarusi across Njemps Kubwa [Liabori], Njemps Ndogo [Lekepir], and Korvan, comprising 16 clans from 6 tribes); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Cust (1883, Vol. I, pp. 149–152), Höhnel (1894), Johnston (1902), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), and Beech (1911).

languages.name: Pokot (Pökoot)
languages.notes: Highland Nilotes (Northern Kalenjin branch, historically Suk / Bawgott across 11 geographical divisions and 24 orten clans; reflexive/middle/emphatic enclitic pronounced [kɛːx] with a final velar fricative and written as a separate word in the Pökoot Bible per Zwarts, Chelimo & Jerono 2024: 539–540); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Johnston (1902), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Beech (1911), Barton (1921), Rottland (1982), and Zwarts, Chelimo & Jerono (2024).

languages.name: Taveta (Kitaveta)
languages.notes: Northeast Coast Bantu (Pare-Taveta group) around Taveta and Lake Jipe; documented in Höhnel (1894), Steggall (1892–1906), Hollis (1910–1911), Johnston (1919), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Daasanach (Dhaasanac)
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic (Western Omo-Tana) agropastoral and fishing community around Ileret on the northeastern shore of Lake Turkana; documented in Höhnel (1894 as Reshiat), Sasse (1974, 1976), Tosco (2001), Nishiguchi (2004), and Blažek (2011).

officialLanguages.role: Language of government, courts, higher education, and media (Article 7(2), Constitution of Kenya 2010)
National lingua franca, parliamentary co-official language, and primary language of inter-ethnic communication (Article 7(1)–(2), Constitution of Kenya 2010)

officialLanguages.language: Kenyan Sign Language (KSL), Braille & Indigenous Languages
officialLanguages.role: Protected and promoted by the State under Article 7(3) of the Constitution of Kenya 2010
